name: Dorothea 'Dory' Oudekerk
languages: Dutch (the farm kind, from her grandmother, and the Bible kind, from church)
equipment: Leather jacket: a heavy cowhide work coat, her father's, cut down, worn over her one black dress
Crowbar: an ice-house pry bar from the ice harvest at Stuyvesant, which she brought because her grandmother told her to
Double-barrel shotgun (12-gauge), her brother Jan's bird gun, in a canvas case
The Oudekerk family Bible, Dutch, 1790, with the family register in the front in five hands, and a letter folded in it
A carpetbag with a nightgown, a shawl, a change of stockings and a pound of her own butter wrapped in a cabbage leaf for whoever is kind to her
A clasp knife, a twist of tobacco for her brothers, and a pair of skates she was taking to be sharpened in Hudson
Mr. Strick's letter, read so often it is coming apart at the folds
features: Hard to Kill (Roughneck: once per long rest, drop to 1 hit point instead of 0; ignore your first level of exhaustion; advantage on CON saves against exhaustion, cold and hard labor)
Heavy Work (Roughneck: advantage on STR checks to lift, push, pull, break or force something, a door, a coffin lid, a fallen beam; carry an unconscious adult at full speed)
Bull-Headed (Roughneck, 2nd level: once per short rest, turn a failed fear check into anger: no Dread, but next turn you must go at the source or break whatever stands between you and it)

Up Before Dawn (Farm-Raised origin: a long rest takes 6 hours; can't be surprised while awake in the last hour before sunrise; advantage on saves against exhaustion from hard work, cold and lost sleep; notices without a check when animals are frightened or wrong)

Hired On (Farmhand background: at any farm in the county she can get a meal and a place in the barn for a day's work, and farm people talk to her as an equal; she notices without a check when a farm's rhythm is wrong: chores undone, stock unfed, a field nobody will work)

personality.traits: I do not talk much and I do not like being talked down to. I work while other people are deciding what to do. I eat everything I am given and say thank you for it.
personality.ideals: What is yours is yours and what is not is not, and a promise to the dead is a promise. My grandmother said so, and she was right about everything.
personality.bonds: My brothers Jan and Hendrick and the farm at Claverack, which has a mortgage due in November that we cannot pay. My grandmother Marritje, dead thirteen years, who made me promise something. The Bible.
personality.flaws: I am stubborn past sense. When I am frightened I get angry, and when I am angry I hit things, and some of them are expensive. I do not trust rich people and I have never met a poor one in this house.

appearance: A broad, strong, weather-burned woman of thirty with a square plain face, steady grey-blue eyes, straw-coloured hair in a thick plait pinned round her head, big red hands with ice-harvest scars across the knuckles, and a cut-down cowhide coat over a black dress that does not fit her. She looks, if anyone in Haverkill had a daguerreotype to compare, a great deal like someone.
backstory: Dorothea Oudekerk was born in 1863 on her family's farm at Claverack in Columbia County, thirty miles up the river from Haverkill, the granddaughter of Marritje Roelofs Oudekerk, who came up from Haverkill as a bride in 1844 and never went back. She works the farm with her two brothers in summer and cuts ice on the river at Stuyvesant in winter with the men, for wages, and she is better at it than most of them. Her grandmother raised her and died in 1880, and made her promise one thing: 'If ever anybody from that house sends for you, you go, and you say her name in it.' Whose name, Dory did not understand until she opened the family Bible after Mr. Strick's letter came. In the register, in her grandmother's hand: 'Sabina, my sister, went up to the stone house October 4 1852 and never came home. She did not drown. M.' And folded in the back, a letter dated Haverkill, 2 October 1852, in a broad quick hand signed with a little drawn anchor: 'Dear Marritje. A. has been signing my name. I go down to Poughkeepsie to the courts on Monday, by the road, not the boat. If you do not hear from me by Sunday, come down with Jan and ask for me at the Landing. Your loving sister, Sabina.' Nobody came. Marritje was ill with her first child, and the next news was that Sabina had drowned. The will calls Dory 'my cousin' and asks her pardon, and she has come to find out what for. (Hooks: CLUES D5 and F2 are in her Bible from the start; she is Sabina's heir and the codicil's beneficiary; Annetje Vedder will know her face; she cannot say the name in the rite for the Greywicks, but she can stand in the room. The GM should let the player decide when to show the Bible.)
